chunks: "Charging and monitoring ICs are important because a lithium cell has to be controlled very precisely, and getting it wrong is both a life and a safety problem.
A charger IC does the whole charge profile on its own. It checks the cell, pre-charges a deeply discharged one gently, runs constant current up to 4. 2 volts, holds 4.
2 volts with something like plus or minus 0. 5 to 1 percent accuracy while the current tapers, then terminates.
It also reads an NTC so it won't charge when it's too hot or cold, runs a safety timer, handles input overvoltage, and often limits its own temperature.

A protection IC, typically with two back-to-back MOSFETs, watches the cell for overvoltage, undervoltage, overcurrent and short circuit, and disconnects within microseconds to milliseconds without any firmware.
A fuel gauge measures voltage, current and temperature and does the state-of-charge and health estimation.
In multi-cell packs there's an analog front end that measures every cell and drives the balancing.

You could build these from discrete parts, but you'd struggle to match the voltage accuracy, you'd need certification, you'd use more board area, and each safety function would need its own validation.
The IC gives a known, tested behavior, smaller size, lower cost at volume, and it works even when the MCU hangs. That's why basically every battery product uses them."
